Guides

FAQ & roadmap

Production readiness, TypeScript, websockets, uploads, Node versions, framework comparisons, the roadmap and contributing.

Is it production-ready?#

It is small and tested, and the behaviour it implements is deliberate. It is also new. The honest position:

  • It works. There is a real test suite and a runnable demo app.
  • It has not seen years of hostile traffic the way Express has.
  • It ships no ecosystem, so anything beyond the built-in middleware is yours to write.

It is a good fit for internal services, prototypes, edge and embedded targets, and any project that values a zero-dependency core. Evaluate it against your own workload before putting it in front of users; nothing here replaces that judgement.

Does it work with TypeScript?#

There are no bundled type declarations. routiva ships as plain ESM JavaScript. You have three options:

  1. Set "allowJs": true and let TypeScript infer what it can from the source.
  2. Write a .d.ts file for the surface you use.
  3. Write the server in plain JavaScript.

The API is regular: classes, named exports and middleware factories. Nothing relies on dynamic shapes that resist typing, so hand-written declarations are straightforward. Bundled types are on the roadmap.

Does it support WebSockets or HTTP/2?#

Not directly. routiva builds on node:http, and app.listen() returns the underlying http.Server, so you can attach a WebSocket library to its upgrade event. There is no HTTP/2 support and none is planned for the zero-dependency core.

Is there a template engine?#

No. There is no res.render(), no view engine setting and no app.locals. You compose HTML in a function and send it:

js
app.get('/', (req, res) => {
  res.type('html').send(`<h1>Hello</h1>`);
});

Escape any user input you interpolate yourself. If you need a full template engine, pair routiva with a standalone renderer or choose Express, where res.render() is integrated.

How do I handle file uploads?#

There is no multipart parser. raw() gives you the request body as a Buffer and text() gives it to you as a string, so a single-part upload can be read directly:

js
app.post('/upload', raw({ limit: '5mb' }), (req, res) => {
  res.json({ bytes: req.body.length });
});

For multipart/form-data, parse the body yourself or run a standalone parsing step. There is no upload middleware in the box, and adding one would bring in the kind of dependency routiva avoids. raw() still enforces a size limit.

Which Node versions are supported?#

Node 18 and newer, matching "engines": { "node": ">=18" }. The runtime uses standard Node modules (node:http, node:fs, node:path, node:zlib, and friends), all present on 18. The test suite relies on global fetch and node:test, which are also 18+. There is no build step, so any current LTS or newer works.

How is it different from Fastify, Hono or Koa?#

routivaFastifyHonoKoa
Runtime dependencies0somesomesome
TargetNode node:httpNodemulti-runtimeNode
Schema validationnobuilt innono
TypeScript typesnot bundledyesyescommunity
Middleware modelone ordered stackhooks and pluginsone stackonion
OpinionExpress-likeplugin-firsttiny and portableminimal

Koa replaces req and res with its own context and uses onion middleware. Fastify adds schemas, plugins and serialization. Hono targets edge runtimes and other platforms. routiva keeps Express's stack and handler signatures and stops there.

How do I report a bug or contribute?#

Open an issue or a pull request on GitHub: github.com/uditc0derr/routiva. A useful bug report has a minimal reproduction, the Node version and what you expected to happen. There is no CLA.

Roadmap#

Ideas that fit the architecture without breaking the zero-dependency rule, in no committed order:

  • res.render() with a pluggable engine interface.
  • A streaming-safe compression path that wraps the socket, not just res.send.
  • Signed cookies and a lightweight session() store.
  • A full app.mount() with sub-app semantics.
  • Bundled TypeScript declarations.
  • Coverage reporting in CI.

None of these has a date. If one matters to you, say so in an issue.

Contributing#

  • Repository: uditc0derr/routiva
  • Package: routiva on npm
  • License: MIT

Run npm test before opening a pull request. Keep the dependency count at zero: if a Node built-in can do it, use the built-in. Match the existing file layout and the one-layer-per-handler model. Small, focused changes are easier to review than broad rewrites.
